(p-244) Surah Bani Isra'il is Meccan, and it has one hundred and ten verses according to the Basran count, and eleven verses according to the Kufan and Syrian counts.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: Subhan (tanzih, the declaration that Allah is exalted above every imperfection) is a proper noun used for the meaning of tasbih (glorification), like 'Uthman as a man's name. Its grammatical position (nasb) is due to a verb that is understood but omitted from speech; its implied form is: "I glorify Allah, subhana (glorifying)." Then subhana was treated as if it were a verb, so it took the place of the verb and conveyed emphatic declaration of Allah's transcendence. ﴿Who took His servant by night﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ). Asra and sara are two dialectal forms. ﴿By night﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time. He restricted it to the night, although the night journey (isra') can only occur at night, either for emphasis, or so that the indefinite wording indicates that the duration of the journey was short, and that he was taken during part of the night from Makkah to Syria, a journey of forty nights. ﴿From the Sacred Mosque﴾: It is said that he was taken from the house of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib. The meaning of "the Sacred Mosque" is the Haram, because it encompasses the mosque and is associated with it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that "the whole Haram is a mosque." It is also said that it is the Sacred Mosque itself, and this is the apparent meaning, for the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was in the Sacred Mosque, in al-Hijr beside the House, between sleeping and waking, Jibril came to me with al-Buraq, and I was then ascended to the heaven on that night." The ascent (mi'raj) from him was from Bayt al-Maqdis. He informed the Quraysh about their caravan, the number of its camels and its conditions, and he also informed them about what he saw in the heavens of wonders, (p-245) that he met the Prophets, peace be upon them, and reached the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) and the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha). The Isra' took place one year before the Hijrah, and it happened while he was awake. It is related from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "By Allah, the body of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not missing, but his spirit was taken up." And similarly from Mu'awiyah. The majority hold the first view, since there is no excellence for one who dreams nor distinction for one who sleeps. ﴿To the farthest mosque﴾: this is Bayt al-Maqdis, because at that time there was no mosque beyond it. ﴿Whose surroundings We have blessed﴾: meaning the blessings of religion and of the world, because it is the place of worship of the Prophets, peace be upon them, the descent place of revelation, and it is surrounded by flowing rivers and fruitful trees. ﴿That We might show him﴾: i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿of Our signs﴾, which indicate the oneness of Allah and the truthfulness of his prophethood, and by his seeing the heavens and the signs in them. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the sayings, ﴿the All-Seeing﴾ of the deeds. The speech shifted between the third-person and first-person forms: it says "asra," then "barakna," then "innahu huwa," and this is the method of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which is one of the methods of eloquence.

And We gave Moses the Book, and made it [the Book, i.e., the Torah] ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel, that you should not take﴾ — meaning: "that you should not take" (or, with the yā' read by Abu 'Amr, meaning: "lest they take") ﴿besides Me a trustee (wakīl)﴾ — a lord to whom you entrust your affairs.

ذُرِّيَّةَ مَن حَمَلْنا مَعَ نُوحٍ ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ is in the accusative either by way of specification (ikhtisas) or by way of address (nida'), according to those who read "لا تَتَّخِذُوا" with the yā' (ya), as a prohibition, meaning: We said to them, "Do not take besides Me a guardian (wakil)," O "offspring of those whom We carried with Noah." ﴿Indeed he﴾, that is, indeed Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿was a grateful servant﴾ in times of ease and in times of hardship. Shukr (gratitude) is the requiting of a blessing with praise of the Benefactor. It is narrated that he would not eat, drink, or wear anything without saying, "All praise is due to Allah." You are the offspring of those who believed in him and were carried with him, so take him as your model just as your fathers took him as their model. The sign of the rectitude of the sons is the soundness of following the practice of the fathers, and you have known the condition of the fathers there, so be, O sons, likewise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 4:

﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book: "You will surely cause corruption on the earth"﴾ And We revealed to them a revelation that was decreed, i.e., cut off and settled, that they would surely cause corruption on the earth without fail. Al-Kitab (the Book) is the Torah. "Li-tufsidunna" (you will surely cause corruption) is the answer to an omitted oath; or the settled decree took the place of an oath, so that "li-tufsidunna" is its answer, as if he said: "And We swore that you would surely cause corruption on the earth." ﴿Twice﴾: the first of them was the killing of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and the imprisonment of Armiya, peace be upon him, when he warned them of the wrath of Allah; and the second was the killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both, and the intent to kill Isa, peace be upon him. ﴿And you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance﴾: you will surely be arrogant toward obeying Allah, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], and what is meant by it is transgression, oppression, and the domination of the corrupters over the reformers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 5:

﴿So when the promise of the first of them came⦆ — that is, the promise of punishment for the first of them — ﴿We sent against you﴾, that is, We empowered against you ﴿servants of Ours, possessing great might﴾, fierce in battle. He means Sennacherib (Sinjarib) and his armies, or Nebuchadnezzar (Bukhtunassar), or Goliath (Jalut). They killed their scholars, burned the Torah, destroyed the Masjid, and took seventy thousand of them captive. ﴿And they went through the homes⦆ — they roamed through them to raid. al-Zajjaj said: al-Jawsu (searching through) is the seeking of a thing with thoroughness. ﴿And it was a promise to be fulfilled﴾ — and the promise of punishment was a promise that had to be carried out.

﴿Then We gave you back the turn [of fortune] against them﴾, meaning the dominance (al-dawla) and victory (al-ghalaba) over them, over those who were sent against you when you repented and turned back from corruption and arrogance. It was said: this refers to the killing of Bukhtunassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and the rescue of the Children of Israel from their captivity and their wealth, and the return of kingship to them. It was also said: We restored dominance to you through the kingship of Talut (Saul) and the killing of Jalut (Goliath) by Dawud (David). ﴿And We supplied you with wealth and sons, and made you more numerous in manpower (nafir)﴾, than you had been. Here (أَكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا) is a tamyiz (specification, a noun clarifying the comparison). Nafir is the plural of nafar, meaning those who go out with a man from among his people.

(p-247)

If you do good, you do good for your own souls; and if you do evil, it is for them. [Qur'an 17:7, first part, plainly rendered:] ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, then it is for them.﴾ It was said that the lam (ل) here means ʿalā (على, "upon"), like His saying ﴿And upon it is what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. But the sound view is that it retains its own meaning, because the lam indicates specification (ikhtisas), and the doer is specifically recompensed for his deed, whether it is good (ḥasanah) or evil (sayyi'ah). That is, good and evil are specific to your own souls; their benefit and harm do not extend to others.

It is related from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I have never done good to anyone, nor done evil to anyone," and he recited ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾, meaning the promise of the final time, ﴿We will send against you [others] to disfigure your faces﴾. Here ﴿Your faces﴾ is the object, and it is omitted because its mention earlier points to it; that is, so that they make the traces of harm and gloom visible in them, like His saying ﴿The faces of those who disbelieved will be disgraced﴾ [al-Mulk: 27].

"Liyasū'" (لِيَسُوءَ) is read by Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī), Ḥamzah and Abū Bakr, with the pronoun referring to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or to the promise, or to the sending. "Linasū'" (لِنَسُوءَ) is read by ʿAlī.

﴿And that they enter the Masjid [in Jerusalem] as they entered it the first time, and that they destroy with complete destruction whatever they overpowered﴾. "Mā ʿalaw" (ما عَلَوْا) is the object of "liyutabbirū" (لِيُتَبِّرُوا), meaning: that they destroy everything they overcame and gained control over; or it may mean the period of their ascendancy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 8:

﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ after the second time, if you repent a further repentance and desist from sins. ﴿But if you return﴾ a third time, ﴿We will return﴾ to punishing you. They did return, so God brought back retribution upon them by setting over them the Persian kings (al-akasira) and imposing tribute upon them. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that the believers were set over them until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We have made Hell a prison (ḥaṣīr) for the disbelievers﴾, a place of confinement. It is said that for prison one says maḥṣar and ḥaṣīr.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright.﴾ That is, to the state that is the most upright of states and the most sound, which is the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) of God, belief in His messengers, and acting in obedience to Him. Or it means to the religious community (milla) or to the path (tariqa).

﴿And gives good news to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾. "Wa-yabshuru" is read by Hamza and ʿAlī. ﴿that for them﴾, meaning "with the fact that for them", ﴿is a great reward﴾, i.e., Paradise. (p-248)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 10:

﴿And that those﴾ and [it is good news] that ﴿who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, ﴿We have prepared﴾, i.e., We have prepared (the original form being aʿdadnā, the dāl changed into the tāʾ, so it became aʿtadnā), ﴿for them a painful punishment﴾, meaning: the Fire. The verse refutes the doctrine of the intermediate position (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn), since it mentions the believers and their reward, and the disbelievers and their reward, and does not mention the grave sinners (al-fasaqah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 11:

﴿And man invokes evil as he invokes good﴾. That is: he calls upon God in his anger for evil against himself, his family, his property and his children, just as he calls upon Him for good for them. Or it means: he seeks immediate benefit, however small, at the cost of a future harm, however great. ﴿And man is ever hasty﴾: he rushes to seek everything that occurs to his heart and crosses his mind, without deliberating over it with the care of one who reflects. Or, by "man" is meant the disbeliever, who invokes punishment mockingly and hastens for it, just as he invokes good when adversity touches him. ﴿And man is ever hasty﴾ means: the punishment will certainly come to him, so why this haste?

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with him both), it was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith who said: ﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], the verse through its end. He was answered, and his neck was struck in patient execution (ṣabran).

As for the omission of the waw from "yadʿu" in the script, it conforms to the pronunciation (muwafaqat al-lafz).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 12:

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs; then We effaced the sign of the night, and We made the sign of the day to be seeing﴾ That is: the night and the day are two signs in themselves. The idafa (construct phrase) in "the sign of the night" and "the sign of the day" is then explanatory (li-l-tabyin), like the idafa of a number to what is counted (ka-idafat al-'adad ila al-ma'dud). That is: We effaced the sign which is the night, and We made the sign which is the day to be seeing. Or: We made the two luminaries of the night and the day two signs, meaning the sun and the moon. We effaced the sign of the night, which is the moon, in that We did not create for it a ray like the ray of the sun, so that things are seen by it with clear sight. And We made the sun to have a ray by whose light everything is seen.

﴿So that you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾ So that by the whiteness of the day you may reach the conducting of your livelihoods. ﴿And that you may know﴾ by the alternation of the two renewals ﴿the number of years and the reckoning﴾, meaning: the reckoning of the terms and the seasons of deeds. Had they been alike, the night would not have been distinguished from the day, and the greedy earners and merchants would not have rested. ﴿And every thing﴾ of what you need in your ﻿religion and your worldly affairs ﴿We have explained in detail﴾ We made it clear with an explanation free of ambiguity, so We removed your excuses, and We left you no argument against Us.

﴿And every person We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾ — his deed — ﴿to his neck﴾. He means: his deed is attached to him in the way a necklace or a shackle is attached to the neck, not to be removed from it. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find laid open﴾. The phrase ﴿yalqāhu﴾ is a description of ﴿kitāban﴾; ﴿yulaqqāhu﴾ is read by Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī). ﴿Manshūran﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿yalqāhu﴾; he means: unfolded, so that he is able to read it. Or the two are two descriptions of the record. And it will be said to him: [...]

"Read your record. Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this day."

﴿اقْرَأْ كِتابَكَ﴾ means: the book of your deeds. Everyone will be raised as one who reads [his record].

﴿كَفى بِنَفْسِكَ اليَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ﴾: the bā' (ب) is extra (zā'idah, redundant, added for emphasis), meaning: "your soul suffices."

﴿حَسِيبًا﴾ is a tamyīz (specification of the noun, accusative of specification). It has the meaning of ḥāsib (one who reckons). ʿAlā (عَلى) is connected to it from your saying: ḥasiba ʿalayhi kadhā (he reckoned that against him). Alternatively, it has the meaning of "sufficient" (al-kāfī), placed in the position of "witness" (al-shahīd), so it takes ʿalā, because a witness suffices the claimant in what concerns him. It is masculine (dhakkara ḥasīban) because it stands in the position of the witness, the judge and the ruler, since generally these matters are undertaken by men. So it is as if it were said: "Your soul suffices as a reckoner, a man." Or the nafs (soul) is interpreted as the person (al-shakhṣ).

Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its own detriment. (That is:) for him is the reward of being guided, and upon him is the burden of going astray.

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.﴾ (That is:) every soul carries a burden, so it bears only its own burden, not the burden of another soul.

﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger.﴾ (That is:) it is not fitting for Us to punish a people with a punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) in this world except after We send to them a messenger who establishes the proof against them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 16:

﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾, i.e., the people of a town, ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾, its pampered ones and its tyrants, ﴿to obedience﴾, according to Abu 'Amr and al-Zajjaj. ﴿But they commit wickedness therein﴾, i.e., they go out of the command, as when you say, "I commanded him, but he disobeyed." Or "amarna" means "We multiply," and its evidence is the recitation of Ya'qub (p-250) "āmarnā." And from this is the hadith: "The best of wealth is a well-tended irrigation channel and a prolific mare" (sikkatun ma'būrah wa muhratun ma'mūrah), i.e., one with abundant offspring. ﴿So the word becomes due against them﴾, i.e., the threat becomes binding upon them, ﴿so We destroy them with complete destruction﴾, i.e., We annihilate them with annihilation.

﴿And how many﴾ is the object (maf'ul) of ﴿We destroyed [of] generations﴾. ﴿How many﴾ is explained by (bayan, explicative apposition) ﴿after Noah﴾, meaning: ʿAd, Thamud and others. ﴿And your Lord is sufficient as Knower of the sins of His servants﴾, even if they concealed them in their breasts, ﴿and Seeing﴾, even if they drew the veils over them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 18:

﴿Whoever desires the hastening (world), We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish.﴾ "What We will" (مَا نَشَاءُ), not "what he wills" (مَا يَشَاءُ). ﴿For whom We wish﴾ (لِمَن نُرِيدُ) is a substitute (badal) for "for him" (لَهُ), with the preposition repeated; it is badal al-ba'd min al-kull (partial substitution from the whole), since the pronoun refers back to "whoever" (مَن). That is: whoever has the hastening (al-'ajilah) as his only concern and does not desire anything other than it, like the disbelievers — We bestow upon him from its benefits what We will, upon whom We wish. Thus He restricts what is hastened to His will, and the one for whom it is hastened to His desire. And such is the situation: you see many of these people wishing for what they wish, yet they are given only a part of it, and many of them wish for that part and are denied it. So there gathers upon them the poverty of this world and the poverty of the Hereafter. As for the believing God-fearing person (al-mu'min al-taqiyy), he has chosen the richness of the Hereafter; so if he is given a portion of this world, it is well and good, and if not, poverty may well be better for him. ﴿Then We have made for him Hell﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿he will enter it (yaslaha)﴾, entering it, ﴿blamed (madhmuman)﴾, despised (mamqutan), ﴿expelled (madhhuran)﴾, driven away (matrudan) from the mercy of Allah.

﴿Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it﴾: "it" is the direct object (mafʿūl bihi), i.e., its due portion of striving and its adequate measure of righteous deeds. ﴿and is a believer﴾: one who affirms God in His promise and His threat. ﴿those—their striving will be appreciated﴾: accepted by God, and rewarded for it.

It is related from some of the salaf (the early pious generations): "Whoever does not have three things, his deed will not benefit him: firm faith, a sincere intention, and correct action." He then recited the verse, for in it He stipulated three conditions for the striving to be thankworthy: the desire for the Hereafter, striving in what one has been charged with, and firm faith.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 20:

﴿Kullan﴾: each one of the two groups. The tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun that is omitted after it (the mudaf ilayhi), and it is in the accusative case, governed by His words ﴿We extend to these﴾, which is a substitute (badal) for kullan. That is: We extend to these ﴿and these﴾, i.e., those who desire the hasty life (al-ʿajilah) and those who desire the Hereafter (al-akhirah), ﴿from the bounty of your Lord﴾, i.e., His provision. The min is connected to numidd (We extend). The ʿata' (bounty) is a noun for what is given, meaning: We increase them from Our bounty, and We make what comes later a supply (madad) for what came earlier, not cutting it off. Thus We provide for both the obedient and the disobedient, out of grace (ʿala wajh al-tafadul). ﴿And the bounty of your Lord has never been forbidden﴾, i.e., withheld (mamnuʿan) from His servants, even if they disobey.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 21:

﴿Look﴾ with the eye of consideration ﴿how We have favoured some of them over others﴾ in wealth, rank, provision and perfection. ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference﴾.

It is related that a group of the nobles and those below them gathered at the door of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him. Permission to enter was given to Bilal and Suhayb, and this grieved Abu Sufyan. Suhayl ibn ʿAmr said: "We were only brought in from our own side. They were called, and we were called" — meaning to Islam — "and they hastened while we delayed. And this is the door of ʿUmar, so how can there be disparity in the Hereafter?!" And if you envy them for the door of ʿUmar, then [consider] what Allah has prepared for them in Paradise is greater.

Address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but what is meant is his community (ummah).

﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit down reproached and forsaken.﴾ That is, lest you end up bearing upon yourself blame and abandonment. It is also said: "reviled with humiliation, deprived of help," since al-khidhlan (abandonment) is the opposite of al-nasr (victory) and al-'awn (aid). The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 160], where He mentioned al-khidhlan in contrast to al-nasr.

﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ and commanded a matter that is definitively settled, ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾. Here *an* (أنْ) is *mufassira* (explanatory, introducing an explanation of the decree). *Wa-lā taʿbudū* (ولا تَعْبُدُوا) is a *nahy* (prohibition), or the phrase means "that you not worship." ﴿And to parents, kindness﴾, meaning "and be kind to your parents," or "that you be kind to your parents." ﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. Here *immā* (إمّا) is the conditional *in* (إنِ) with *mā* added to it for emphasis, which is why the emphatic *nūn* (النون المؤكدة) enters the verb. If *in* were used alone, the emphatic *nūn* could not enter it. You do not say *in tukrimanna Zaydan yukrimka*, but rather *immā tukrimannahu*. ﴿One of them﴾ is the subject of *yablughanna*. In the reading of Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, it is *yablughānn*, where *aḥadahumā* is a substitute (*badal*) for the *alif* of the pronoun referring to the two parents. ﴿Or both of them﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to *aḥadahumā*, either as a subject or as a substitute. ﴿Then do not say to them, "Uff"﴾. According to Madanī and Ḥafṣ it is *uffin*; Makkī and Shāmī read *uffa*; the others read *uffu*. It is an exclamation indicating impatience. The kasra is the original form, arising from the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn*). The fatḥa is for lightness, and the tanwīn indicates indefiniteness, meaning "I am impatient with an impatience." Omitting it indicates definiteness, meaning "I am impatient with the known impatience." ﴿And do not scold them﴾, that is, do not rebuke them for what they do that does not please you. *Al-nahy* (the forbidding) and *al-nahr* (the rebuking) are brothers in meaning. ﴿And speak to them﴾ in place of the reproach and the rebuke, ﴿a generous word﴾, that is, a gentle, pleasant word, as good manners require. Alternatively, it means that you say, "O my father, O my mother," and do not address them by their names, for that is a form of discourtesy. There is no harm in doing so in other circumstances, as ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Abū Bakr gave me such-and-such." The benefit of *ʿindaka* (with you) is that when they become a burden upon their child, with no one else to care for them, they are in his home and under his protection, and that is more burdensome for him. Therefore he is commanded to adopt gentleness of character toward them, so that when something irritates him, he does not say to them what he finds disgusting, "Uff," let alone anything more than that. Allah, glorified is He, has greatly emphasized the injunction concerning them, beginning it by pairing kindness to them with His own tawḥīd, then restricting the matter of observing their rights so that He does not permit even the least word that escapes from one who is impatient, even amid the causes of impatience and circumstances in which a person can hardly remain patient.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 24:

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾, meaning: lower to them your wing, as He said, ﴿and lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88]. He attributed the wing to humility (dhull) just as Hatim (al-Ta'i) is attributed to generosity (judd). The meaning is: lower to them your humble wing ﴿out of mercy﴾, from the abundance of your mercy towards them and your tenderness toward them because of their old age and their need today for one who was, in the past, the neediest of God's creation in need of them. (p-253) Al-Zajjaj said: Lower your side, humbling yourself before them, out of your great mercy towards them. ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small.﴾ Do not be content with your mercy towards them, which has no permanence, but call upon God to show them His everlasting mercy, and make this a recompense for their mercy towards you in your childhood and their rearing of you. The address is directed to someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ), and the supplication is specific to the two parents who are Muslims. It was said: if they are both disbelievers, he may seek mercy for them on condition of faith, and pray to God to guide them.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The pleasure of God lies in the pleasure of the two parents, and His displeasure lies in their displeasure." It is also related: "The dutiful one may do whatever he wishes, and he will not enter the Fire; and the disobedient one may do whatever he wishes, and he will not enter Paradise." And from him (ﷺ): "Beware of disobedience to the two parents, for the fragrance of Paradise can be smelled from a distance of a thousand years, yet it will not be smelled by a disobedient child, nor by one who severs the ties of kinship, nor by an old adulterer, nor by one who trails his garment out of arrogance. Indeed, greatness belongs to God, Lord of the worlds."

Your Lord knows best what is in your souls: what is in your hearts of intention to do good to your parents, and of eagerness and generosity in serving them. ﴿If you are righteous﴾, intending goodness and kindness, but a lapse occurs from you in a state of anger or when the chest is constricted, a slip that leads to harming them, and then you turn back (ṣāliḥīn) to God and seek forgiveness for it, ﴿then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back often﴾. The awwāb (al-awwāb, one who often turns back) is the one who, when he sins, hastens to repentance. It is permissible that this be general for everyone from whom a wrong has occurred and who then repents from it, and it includes the one who wrongs his parents and repents from his wrongdoing, since it comes after it (i.e., the verse follows the mention of the wrong and its remedy).

**"And give the near of kin his due"** (﴿وَآتِ ذا القُرْبى﴾) from you, **"his right"** (﴿حَقَّهُ﴾), i.e., the maintenance (al-nafaqah) when they are mahram relatives who are poor; **"and the poor and the wayfarer"** (﴿والمِسْكِينَ وابْنَ السَبِيلِ﴾), i.e., give these their right from the zakat. **"And do not squander wastefully"** (﴿وَلا تُبَذِّرْ تَبْذِيرًا﴾), and do not be extravagant, extravagance (israf).

It has been said: tabdhir (squandering, tabdhir) is dispersing wealth in what is not lawful or not in its proper place. On the authority of Mujahid: "If one spends a mudd (a unit of measure, mudd) on falsehood, that is squandering." Some people spent an expenditure on good, and spent more, and his companion said to him: "There is no good in extravagance." He said: "There is no extravagance in good."

Verse 27 of Surah 17 is not translated here as a standalone quotation; the passage below is Nasafi's commentary on it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 27:**

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾, meaning: like them in wickedness, and this is the utmost of blame, for there is no evil worse than that of the Devil. Or it means they are their brothers and friends, because they obey them in what they command them of extravagance. ﴿And the Devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾. So he should not be obeyed, for he calls only to the likes of his own deed.

"And if you turn away from them" — meaning: and if you turn away from the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer out of shame at refusing them, ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾ — that is: and if you turn away from them due to the lack of provision from your Lord, which you hope will be opened up for you — so He called provision "mercy" — then ﴿repel them with gentle words﴾ (rudda jamilan). He placed ﴿seeking﴾ (al-ibtigha') in the position of ﴿lack﴾ (al-fuqd), because one who lacks provision is one who seeks it. So the lack was the cause of the seeking, and the seeking was caused by it; thus the effect (al-musabbab) was placed in the position of the cause (al-sabab). It is said: "yusira al-amr" and "usira al-amr" (the matter became easy or difficult), like "su'ida al-rajul" and "nuhisa" (the man was made happy or unlucky), so it is passive (maf'ul).

It was also said that its meaning is: ﴿then say to them: "God has provided for us and for you from His bounty,"﴾ in the sense that it is a supplication for them that eases their poverty for them, as if its meaning were: "a word that is accompanied by ease (maysur)," and that is ease (al-yusr), i.e., a supplication containing ease.

"Ibtigha'" is either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and "turjuha" is a circumstantial clause (hal).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 29:

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ "Kull" (كُلَّ) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq), because it is annexed to the word that follows it (al-bast). This is a metaphor for withholding from the miserly person and giving to the extravagant one, and it is a command to moderation (iqtisad), which lies between extravagance (israf) and stinginess (taqtir). ﴿So you sit reproached﴾: you will become blameworthy before Allah, because the extravagant person is not pleasing to Him, and before people. The poor man says: "He gave to so-and-so and deprived me," and the rich man says: "He does not manage the affairs of livelihood well." And before yourself: when you are in need and regret what you have done. ﴿Destitute﴾ (mahsuran): cut off from you, with nothing in your possession. It comes from hasarahu al-safar (the journey wore him out), when it has left a severe effect on him, or "naked," from hasara ra'sahu (he uncovered his head). A Muslim woman once contended with her Jewish co-wife (p-255) that he, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), was more generous than Moses (peace be upon him). So she sent her daughter to ask him for the shirt he was wearing, and he gave it to her and sat naked. Then the prayer was called, but he did not go out for the prayer, and so this verse was revealed.

Then He consoled the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by informing him that this (the restriction of provision) is not because of any contempt on His part toward him, nor out of stinginess toward him. Rather, because the expansion and measure of provisions are entrusted to Allah the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills﴾, so the extension is not up to you. ﴿And He restricts it﴾, i.e., He constricts it, so there is no blame upon you. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾: Acquainted (khabir) with their interests, so He carries them out; Seeing (basir) with their needs, so He fulfills them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 31:

﴿And do not kill your children﴾ — their killing their children, i.e., burying their daughters alive (wa'd), ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ — i.e., destitution. ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ — He forbade them from that and guaranteed their provision. ﴿Indeed, their killing is a great sin (khiti'an kabiran)﴾ — a great sin. It is said: khati'a khit'an, like atham ithman (he sinned, a sin). "Khata'an" is the reading of Ibn 'Amir (Shami), and it is the opposite of correctness (al-sawab); it is a noun from akhta'a (to err). It is also said that it and al-khit' are like al-hadhar and al-hidhr (both meaning caution). "Khita'an" with the madda and the kasra is the reading of Ibn Kathir (Makki).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 32:

﴿And do not approach adultery.﴾ The shortened vowel (al-qasr) is more common in it, and the lengthened vowel (al-madd) is also a valid usage in the language, and it has been recited with it. It is a prohibition against the means that lead to adultery, such as touching, kissing, and the like. Had the intention been to prohibit adultery itself, he would have said: "And do not commit adultery." ﴿Indeed, it is an abomination﴾, a sin that exceeds the bounds of the Sharia and of reason. ﴿And evil is it as a way﴾, and wretched is the way it represents.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 33:

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right.﴾ That is: by committing what makes blood permissible. ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾ — not having committed what makes blood permissible — ﴿We have given his heir authority﴾ — a power over the killer in exacting retribution from him. ﴿So let him not exceed bounds in killing﴾ — the pronoun refers to the heir; that is: let him not kill other than the killer, nor two persons while the killer is one, as was the custom of the people of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). Or the exceeding of bounds is mutilation, and the pronoun refers to the first killer. [The reading] "fa-la tusrif" (﴿So do not exceed bounds﴾) is recited by Hamzah and ʿAli, addressing the heir or the killer of the wronged person. ﴿Indeed, he is ever supported﴾ — the pronoun refers to the heir; that is: it is sufficient for him that Allah has supported him by prescribing retribution for him, so let him not seek more than that. Or it refers to the wronged person, i.e., Allah is his helper, since He prescribed retribution for his killing, and He will help him in the Hereafter with reward. Or it refers to the one whom the heir kills without right and exceeds bounds in killing him, for he is ever supported by the prescription of retribution against the transgressor. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that retribution applies between free person and slave, and between Muslim and dhimmi (protected non-Muslim), because the lives of the people of the dhimma and of slaves are included in the verse by virtue of their being forbidden (to be killed).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 34:

﴿And do not approach the wealth of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ — with the manner and method that is best, which is to guard it and make it grow. ﴿Until he reaches his maturity (ashudd)﴾ — i.e., eighteen years. ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾ — by the commands of Allah the Exalted and His prohibitions. ﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever questioned﴾ — meaning demanded: it is demanded of the one who made the covenant that he not neglect it and that he fulfill it; or, the meaning is that the one who made the covenant will be questioned (about it).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 35:

﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance.﴾ With kasr on the qaf (al-qistas, pronounced al-qisṭās): Hamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafs read it so. It is every balance, small or large, of the scales for dirhams and other things. It is also said that it is the qurusṭūn, i.e. the qubbān (steelyard). ﴿al-mustaqīm﴾: the upright, the balanced. ﴿That is better﴾ in the world, ﴿and better in outcome﴾ (taʾwīl), meaning consequence. It is on the pattern of taf'īl from āla, when it returns, and it is what a matter comes back to and ends in.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 36:

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ — i.e., do not pursue what you do not know. That is: do not say, "I saw," when you did not see, or "I heard," when you did not hear. And from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: do not bear false witness. And from Ibn 'Abbas: do not accuse anyone of what you do not know. Relying on mere conjecture (mubtil al-ijtihad) is not valid in this, because that is a kind of knowledge. ﴿And if you know them to be believers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. The Lawgiver has made preponderant assumption (ghalib al-zann) stand in the place of knowledge and ordered that it be acted upon, as in testimony. Our basis for acting on the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) is what we have mentioned. ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart — all of those will be held accountable﴾. "Those" refers to hearing, sight and heart, because "ula'ika" may refer to rational beings and also to others, as in the verse of Jarir:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days."

As for "'anhu" (about it), it is in the position of the nominative by being the agent: i.e., each one of them will be questioned about it. So "mas'ul" is attributed to the prepositional phrase, like "al-maghdub" in ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7]. It is said to a person: Why did you listen to what it was not lawful for you to hear? Why did you look at what it was not lawful for you to look at? Why did you resolve upon what it was not lawful for you to resolve upon? Thus [it is stated] in al-Kashshaf, but there is an objection to it by some scholars, because the prepositional phrase takes the place of the agent only when it comes after the verb; when it precedes it, it does not.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 37:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ — (marahan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: while being full of arrogant pride (dhā maraḥin). ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾ — you will never make a rent (kharq) in it by your treading upon it and the heaviness of your stamping. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾ — by your stretching yourself up, and this is a mockery (tahakkum) of the self-conceited; or it means: you will never equal them in strength. And (ṭūlan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the doer (al-fā'il) or from the object (al-maf'ūl).

﴿كُلُّ ذَلِكَ كانَ سَيِّئُهُ﴾ *(All of that, its evil was...)* is read by the Kufi and Shami reciters as ﴿سَيِّئُهُ﴾, with *sayyi'* in an idafa (genitive annexation) to the pronoun of ﴿كُلُّ﴾ *(kull)*. The others read ﴿سَيِّئَةً﴾. ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ مَكْرُوهًا﴾ *(hateful in the sight of your Lord)*. He made ﴿مَكْرُوهًا﴾ masculine, because ﴿السَيِّئَةَ﴾ in the category of nouns stands in the position of *al-dhanb* (the sin) and *al-ithm* (the transgression). The rule of adjectives has departed from it, so its feminine form is not taken into account. Do you not see that you say *al-zina sayyi'a* (fornication is an evil), just as you say *al-sariqa sayyi'a* (theft is an evil)?

If you say: the qualities mentioned are partly evil and partly good, and for this reason whoever read ﴿سَيِّئُهُ﴾ with the idafa (p-258) meant: whatever of what was mentioned was evil, it was hateful in the sight of God. Then what is the basis for the reading of whoever read ﴿سَيِّئَةً﴾? I say: ﴿كُلُّ ذَلِكَ﴾ is an encompassing of what He forbade in particular, not of all the qualities enumerated.

﴿That﴾ refers to what precedes it, from His saying ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾ up to this final point, ﴿of the wisdom that your Lord has revealed to you﴾, meaning what the intellect judges to be sound and what the soul is made upright by following. ﴿And do not set up with Allah another god, lest you be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾, meaning cast out from mercy. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that these eighteen verses were on the tablets of Musa, peace be upon him. The first of them was "Do not set up with Allah another god," and the last was "rejected." Its opening and its closing were made the prohibition of shirk (associating partners with Allah), because tawhid (the affirmation of Allah's oneness) is the head and the foundation of every wisdom. Whoever lacks it, no wisdom benefits him, even if he surpasses the wise in it and his crown scrapes the sky. Books of wisdom did not avail the philosophers, and they are more astray from the religion of Allah than cattle!?

Then He addressed those who said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," with His words: ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for denunciation (inkar). It means: Has your Lord singled you out, in purity and sincerity, with the best of children, namely sons? ﴿And has He taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ That is, He has taken for Himself the lesser of them, who are daughters. This contradicts wisdom and what your own reasoning holds: slaves are not given the finest and purest of things, while the worst and lowest of things are reserved for masters. ﴿Indeed, you utter a monstrous saying.﴾ This is because you attributed children to Him, and children are among the properties of bodies; then you preferred yourselves over Him, since you assign to Him what you dislike.

And indeed We have varied (repeated) in this Qur'an ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَرَّفْنا في هَذا القُرْآنِ﴾ — that is, [in] the revelation (al-tanzil). The intended meaning is: "And indeed We have varied it" — that is, this meaning, in various places of the revelation — and the pronoun has been omitted because it is understood. ﴿لِيَذَّكَّرُوا﴾ — with the lightened form (al-takhfif), [read by] Hamza and Ali — meaning: We repeated it so that they might be admonished. ﴿وَما يَزِيدُهم إلا نُفُورًا﴾ — [increasing them only in] aversion from the truth. (p-259) Al-Thawri, whenever he recited it, would say: "What has increased me in humble submission to You is what has increased Your enemies in aversion."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 42:

﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say⁠﴾ — "with Him" meaning with Allah. Ibn Kathir (in Mecca) and Hafs (in the reading of ʿĀṣim) read "as they say" with the ya' (يَقُولُونَ, yaqūlūna, "they say" in the third person). ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ — meaning: they would have sought a way to Him who possesses the dominion and lordship, by contention, as kings do with one another; or they would have sought nearness to Him, as in His saying: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord⁠﴾ [al-Isra' 17:57]. "Idhan" (then, in that case) indicates that what follows it, namely "they would have sought," is an answer to the claim of the polytheists and the consequent of "law" (law, "if").

"Glory be to Him, and exalted is He far above what they say" (﴿سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى عَمّا يَقُولُونَ﴾). Ḥamzah and ʿAlī read it with the ta' (تَعالى ... تَعالِيًا), i.e., ﴿تَعالَى﴾ in the past-tense form with the ta' sound.

﴿ʿUluwwan﴾ (عُلُوًّا) means exaltation (taʿālīyan), and the intended meaning is clearing Him of that (what they attribute to Him) and declaring Him free from it (al-barāʾah and al-nazāhah). ﴿Kabīran﴾ (كَبِيرًا), "great," describes the exaltation as being great, as an intensification (mubālaghah) in the meaning of clearing Him and distancing Him from what they ascribe to Him.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 44:**

﴿Tusabbihu﴾ (they glorify), with the letter *ta'* (in the feminine form), is the reading of the Iraqi readers (*qurra'* al-*'Iraq*) other than Abu Bakr. ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whatever is in them glorify Him. There is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise﴾, meaning it says, "Glory be to God and praise be to Him." According to al-Suddi, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No fish is caught in the sea, and no bird flies, except that it is caught because of its neglect of the glorification of God, exalted is He." ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾ is due to the difference of languages, or to the difficulty of perceiving it, or it is a cause for the one who looks at it to glorify God, just as the one who points to good is like the one who does it. The first (explanation) is the preferred one. ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing﴾ toward the ignorance of His servants, ﴿Forgiving﴾ toward the sins of the believers. (p-٢٦٠)

﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier.﴾

Meaning: having a covering, or a barrier that is not seen, so it is "مَسْتُورٌ" (concealed).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 46:

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings (akinna)﴾ the plural of kinan, which is that which conceals a thing. ﴿Lest they understand it﴾ out of aversion to their understanding it. ﴿And in their ears is deafness (waqra)﴾ a heaviness that prevents them from listening. ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an (wahdahu)﴾ it is said wahada, yahidu, wahdan and wahdatan, like wada'a, ya'idu, w'dan and i'datan. So it is a verbal noun (masdar) that takes the place of the circumstantial accusative (hal), its original form being yahidu wahdahu, meaning wahdan. ﴿They turned back on their backs (wallaw 'ala adbarihim)﴾ they returned on their heels. ﴿In aversion (nufuran)﴾ a verbal noun meaning turning away, or the plural of nafir, like qa'id and qu'ud. That is: they like that their idols be mentioned along with Him, because they are polytheists; so when they hear of the Oneness of God, they flee.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 47:

﴿We know best what they listen for when they listen to you﴾. That is: We know best the state or the manner in which they listen to the Qur'an. The Qur'an is the thing listened to, and it is elided; "bihi" (with it) is a circumstantial clause (hal) and an explanation (bayan) of "ma" (what). That is, they listen to the Qur'an mockingly (hazi'in), not seriously (jaddin), whereas it was obligatory upon them to listen to it seriously (jaddin).

﴿when they listen to you﴾: "idh" is in the accusative case, governed by "a'lamu" (We know best). That is: We know best at the time of their listening what they listen for with it.

﴿and when they are in private consultation﴾: and what they confide to one another, when they are people of private consultation (dhawu najwa).

﴿when the wrongdoers say﴾: "idh" here is a substitute (badal) for "idh hum" (when they are).

﴿You follow none but a man bewitched﴾: he was bewitched and so became mad (fa-junna).

Behold how they have coined similitudes for you; so they have gone astray, and they cannot find a way.

They likened you to the poet, the sorcerer, and the madman. "So they have gone astray" means: they went astray in all of that, like one who seeks a path in the wilderness (tih) that he may travel, yet cannot find it; he is bewildered in his affair and does not know what to do.

"And they say," that is, those who deny the resurrection, "When we have become bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?" That is, renewed. "Khalqan" (a new creation) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: created anew.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 50–51:

﴿Say: "Be you stones or iron,﴾ ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts."﴾ That is, the heavens and the earth, for they are greater in your estimation than to accept life. ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?" Say: "He who created you the first time."﴾ That is, He will restore you. The meaning is: you consider it far-fetched that God should renew your creation and return you to the state of life after you were dry bones, even though bones are part of a living being; indeed, they are the pillar of its creation upon which the rest of it is built. So it is no marvel that God, by His power, should return them to their first state. But even if you were the thing furthest from life, namely stones or iron, He would still be able to return you to the state of life. ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾, that is, they will move their heads toward you in wonder and mockery. ﴿And they will say, "When will it be?"﴾, that is, the Resurrection, considering it far-fetched and denying it. ﴿Say: "It may be that it is near"﴾. That is: it is near, and "ʿasā" (it may be) here indicates certainty (li-l-wujub).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 50–51:

﴿Say: "Be you stones or iron,﴾ ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts."﴾ That is, the heavens and the earth, for they are greater in your estimation than to accept life. ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?" Say: "He who created you the first time."﴾ That is, He will restore you.
