Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 52:

﴿The Day He calls you﴾ to the reckoning, which is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and you will respond, praising Him﴾, i.e., you will respond while praising (ḥāmidīn). The bāʾ (in bi-ḥamdihi) is for the state (ḥāl). From Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: they will shake the dust from their heads and say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You." ﴿And you will think you remained only a little﴾, i.e., a brief stay, or a little time in the world, or in the grave.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 53:

﴿And say to My servants﴾ — i.e., say to the believers: ﴿that they should say﴾ to the polytheists ﴿the word which is best﴾, that is, the gentlest and mildest, and that they should not be harsh with them. It is that they say: "May Allah guide you" (yahdikum Allah). ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ — he casts corruption among them and stirs some of them against others, so as to bring about enmity between them. Al-nazgh (incitement, "nazgh") is the instigation of evil and the spoiling of relations between people. Talha read "yanzigh" with a kasra (on the z), and both are two dialects (lughatan) of the same word. ﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been to man a manifest enemy﴾ — clearly, openly hostile.

Or he explained "that which is best" by His saying, ﴿Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾, with guidance and success; ﴿or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ with abandonment (al-khidhlan). That is: they should say to them this word and similar words, and not say to them, "You are among the people of the Fire, you will be punished," and whatever else is similar to this that enrages them and provokes them to evil. His saying, ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ [al-Isra: 53], is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). ﴿And We have not sent you over them as a guardian﴾, meaning, a keeper of their deeds, and their affairs are not entrusted to you. Rather, We have sent you only as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, so be lenient with them and instruct your companions to be patient and tolerant.

Your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth (﴿وَرَبُّكَ أعْلَمُ بِمَن في السَماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾), and of their conditions, and of all that each one of them deserves. ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ (﴿وَلَقَدْ فَضَّلْنا بَعْضَ النَبِيِّينَ عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾). In it there is an indication of the preference of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His saying ﴿And We gave David the Zabur﴾ (﴿وَآتَيْنا داوُدَ زَبُورًا﴾) is evidence of the aspect of his preference, and that he is the Seal of the Prophets, and that his community is the best of communities, because that is written in the Zabur of David. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly written in the Zabur, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 105). They are Muhammad and his community. He did not define the Zabur here, but he defined it in His saying ﴿And We have certainly written in the Zabur﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 105), because it is like al-ʿAbbas and ʿAbbas, and al-Fadl and Fadl.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 56:

﴿Say: Call upon those you claim﴾ (to be gods) ﴿besides Him﴾, besides Allah. They are the angels, or Jesus and ʿUzayr, or a group of jinn whom some people among the Arabs worshipped, after which the jinn embraced Islam without the worshippers realising it. ﴿Then they have no power to remove the harm from you, nor to change it﴾. That is: call upon them, for they are not able to remove from you the harm, whether of illness, poverty or punishment, nor to transfer it from one person to another.

**"Those"** (ʾulāʾika) is the subject (mubtada'). **"Whom they call upon"** (alladhīna yadʿūna) is a relative clause (ṣifah), meaning: they call upon them as gods or worship them. The predicate (khabar) is **"seek, through their Lord, the means"** (yabtaghūna ilā rabbihimu al-wasīlah). The meaning is that those whom they worship themselves seek the means, which is nearness (al-qurbah) to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**"Which of them"** (ayyuhum) is a substitution (badal) for the wāw of "yabtaghūna" (they seek). "Ayy" here is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), meaning: he who is **"nearest"** (aqrab) of them seeks the means to Allah. So how about those who are not nearest? Alternatively, "yabtaghūna al-wasīlah" is taken to include the meaning of "yaḥrişūna" (they eagerly strive), as if it were said: they eagerly strive, which of them would be nearer to Allah, and that is by obedience and increasing in good.

**"And they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment"** — like the other servants of Allah. So how can they claim that they are gods?

**"Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared"** (maḥdhūran): worthy that everyone should beware of it, from a near angel and a sent prophet, let alone others.

﴿There is no town but We shall destroy it before the Day of Resurrection, or We shall punish it with a severe punishment.﴾ It was said: destruction is for the righteous town and punishment is for the wicked town. ﴿That was written in the Book﴾, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), ﴿inscribed﴾, written down.

From Muqatil: I found in the books of al-Dahhak, in his tafsir of this verse: As for Makkah, the Abyssinians will ruin it. Al-Madinah will perish by hunger, al-Basrah by drowning, and al-Kufah by the Turks. The mountains will perish by thunderbolts and quakings. As for Khurasan, its punishment takes many forms. As for Balkh, a collapse will befall them, and its people will perish. As for Badakhshan, peoples will ruin it. As for Tirmidh, its people will die of plague. As for Saghaniyan up to Washjird, they will be killed in a great slaughter. As for Samarqand, the sons of Qantura'a will overcome it and kill its people in a great slaughter; likewise Farghana, al-Shash, Asbijab and Khwarizm. As for Bukhara, it is the land of tyrants, and they will die of drought and hunger. As for Marw, sand will overwhelm it, and its scholars and worshippers will perish there. As for Herat, they will be rained upon with serpents, which will devour them completely. As for Nishapur, its people will be struck by thunder, lightning and darkness, and most of them will perish. As for al-Rayy, the Tabariyya and the Daylam will overcome it and kill them. As for Armenia and Adharbayjan, the hooves of horses, armies, thunderbolts and quakings will destroy them. As for Hamadhan, the Daylam will enter it and ruin it. As for Hulwan, a calm wind will pass over it while its people are asleep, and in the morning its people will have become apes and swine. Then a man from Juhayna will come out and enter Egypt; woe to its people and to the people of Damascus, woe to the people of Ifriqiya, and woe to the people of al-Ramla, but he will not enter Bayt al-Maqdis. As for Sijistan, a violent wind will strike them for days, then a collapse will come upon them, and the scholars will die in it. As for Kirman, Isfahan and Fars (p-264), an enemy will come upon them and they will cry out a cry by which hearts will be torn from their places and bodies will die.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 17, verse 59:

﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them.﴾ The word "prevention" is used metaphorically (*istiʿāra*, metaphor) for the withholding of sending the signs. The first "an" (that) together with its clause (*ṣila*) is in the accusative position, because it is the second object of *manaʿanā* (prevented us). The second "an" together with its clause is in the nominative position, because it is the subject (*fāʿil*) of *manaʿanā*. The underlying construction is: "And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except the denial of the former peoples." The signs meant are those that the Quraysh proposed, such as turning the Safa hill into gold, reviving the dead, and other things. God's established way (*sunna*) regarding the nations is that whoever among them proposes a sign and is granted it, but then does not believe, will be hastened into punishment by total annihilation. The meaning is: nothing prevented Us from sending what they propose of signs except that those like them, those sealed upon their hearts, such as ʿAd and Thamud, denied them. And indeed, had they been sent, they would have denied them as those had, and would have been punished with the annihilating punishment. We have decreed to delay the matter of those to whom you were sent until the Day of Resurrection. Then he mentioned from those signs that the former peoples proposed and then denied when they were sent, and so they were destroyed. One of them was the she-camel of Salih, peace be upon him, because the traces of their destruction are near their borders, visible to those who leave and those who arrive. So He said: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel⦆ in response to their proposal, ﴿as a clear sign⦆, ﴿but they wronged themselves through it⦆, that is, they disbelieved in it. As for ﴿And We do not send the signs⦆: if by them is meant the proposed signs, then the meaning is: We do not send them ﴿except as a warning⦆ of the descent of imminent punishment, like a vanguard and forerunner to it. If they do not fear, the punishment falls upon them. If by them is meant other signs, then the meaning is: And We do not send what We send of signs, such as the verses of the Qur'an and others, except as a warning and a caution of the punishment of the Hereafter. This (*takhwīfan*) is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 17, verse 60:

﴿And when We said to you, "Indeed your Lord encompasses the people. And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people."﴾ (p-265) Recall when We revealed to you that your Lord encompasses Quraysh in knowledge and power, so all of them are in His grip. Therefore do not be concerned about them, proceed with your command, and convey what you were sent with. Or it means: We gave you the good news of the battle of Badr and of victory over them. This is His saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], and His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 12]. He made it as though it had already happened and been found. So He said, "encompasses the people," according to His custom in His reports. Perhaps God Most High showed him their places of death in his dream, for he used to say when he arrived at the water of Badr: "By God, it is as though I am looking at the places where the people will fall." He pointed to the ground and said, "This is the place where so-and-so will fall." Quraysh heard what had been revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about Badr and what he had been shown in his dream of their places of death, so they laughed, mocked, and hastened him with mockery.

﴿And the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾: that is, We did not make the accursed tree in the Qur'an except as a trial for the people. When they heard His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum, the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43-44], they made it a subject of ridicule and said, "Muhammad claims that the Hellfire burns stones, and then he says a tree will grow in it." They did not measure God with His true measure when they said that. It is not impossible that God makes a tree of a kind that fire does not consume. The wool of the salamander, which is a small creature in the lands of the Turks, is made into napkins; when they become soiled, they are thrown into the fire, the dirt burns away, and the napkin remains intact, untouched by the fire. You also see the ostrich swallowing burning coals without being harmed. God created fire in every tree, yet it does not burn them. So it is possible that He creates within the fire a tree that the fire does not burn.

The meaning is: signs are sent only as a warning to the servants. These people were warned of the punishment of this world, which is killing on the day of Badr, and they were warned of the punishment of the Hereafter and of the tree of al-Zaqqum, yet it had no effect on them. Then He said, ﴿And We frighten them﴾, that is, with the frightening things of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿But it increases them only in great transgression﴾: the warning increases them only in transgression. So how can a people in this state fear the sending of the signs they demand?

It is also said that the "vision" is the Night Journey (*al-Isra'*), and the "trial" is the apostasy of those who considered that momentous. Those who say the Night Journey took place in a dream rely on this, and those who say it took place while awake interpret "vision" as "sight." It was called a vision (*ru'ya*) according to the claim of the deniers, when they said to him, "Perhaps it was a dream you saw," considering it unlikely. Just as He named things by their names as the disbelievers used them, as in His saying: ﴿Then he turned to their gods﴾ [al-Saffat: 91], and their saying, "Where are my partners?" Or it is the vision that he would enter Mecca, and the trial is the hindrance at Hudaybiyya.

If you say that the Qur'an does not mention cursing the tree of al-Zaqqum, we reply: its meaning is "and the accursed tree," whose eaters are accursed, and they are the disbelievers, because He said: ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 51], ﴿will surely eat from a tree of al-Zaqqum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 52], ﴿and fill your bellies with it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 53]. So it is described by the cursing of its people in a figurative sense (*al-majaz*). Also, the Arabs say that every disagreeable and harmful food is "accursed." Also, cursing (*al-la'n*) means being distanced from mercy, and the tree is at the root of Hell, in the place farthest from mercy.

هُوَ تَمْيِيزٌ (tamyīz, an accusative of specification) أوْ حالٌ (ḥāl, a circumstantial accusative) مِنَ المَوْصُولِ (al-mawṣūl, the relative pronoun), والعامِلُ فِيهِ أأسْجُدُ (the governing element in it is *a-asjudu*) عَلى: أأسْجُدُ لَهُ وهو طِينٌ (meaning: *a-asjudu lahu wa-huwa ṭīn*, "Am I to prostrate to him while he is clay?"), أيْ: أصْلُهُ طِينٌ (i.e., his origin is clay).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 17, verse 62:

﴿قالَ أرَأيْتَكَ هَذا الَّذِي﴾ *al-kāf* (the particle *ka* in *araʾayta-ka*) has no grammatical position (*mawḍiʿ*), because it is mentioned for address, for emphasis. *Hādhā* is the direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*). The meaning is: "Tell me about this one ﴿whom You have honored over me﴾, that is, whom You have preferred. Why did You honor him over me, ﴿when I am better than him. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾ [Ṣād 38:76]." That part has been omitted for brevity, since what precedes it indicates it. Then he began and said: ﴿If You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize control over his descendants﴾. *Akhkhartan* is read without the *yāʾ* by the Kufan and Syrian readers, and the *lām* is *muwaṭṭi'a* (preparatory), introducing the omitted oath. ﴿I will surely destroy them﴾, meaning I will utterly root them out by leading them astray, ﴿except for a few﴾, who are the sincere ones (*al-mukhlaṣūn*). It has been said: one out of every thousand. The accursed one knew this either through being informed, or because he saw that humans are a creation driven by desire (*khalqun shahwānī*). (p-267)

"Said: Go" — this is not from the going that is the opposite of coming; rather its meaning is: proceed to your affair which you have chosen, by forsaking and abandonment. Then he followed it with mention of what the evil of his choice drew upon him, saying ﴿Whoever among them follows you, then indeed Hell is your recompense﴾. The implied sense is: indeed Hell is their recompense and your recompense. Then the addressed (you, plural) was given precedence over the absent (them), so it was said "your recompense." And ﴿a full recompense﴾ is in the accusative, meaning "in full," with the implied verb "you will be recompensed."

﴿And incite﴾: *istazalla* (to cause to slip) or *istakhaffa* (to make light). *Istafazzahu* means *istakhaffahu*, he made him light-headed, and *al-fazz* is the light-minded one.

﴿Whomever you can among them with your voice﴾: through whispering, or through singing, or through the *mizmar* (a wind instrument).

﴿And muster against them﴾: gather them and shout at them. *Al-jalaba* is the shouting, from *ajlib*.

﴿With your horsemen and your footmen﴾: with every rider and walker among the people of corruption. *Al-khayl* refers to horsemen (*al-khayyala*), and *al-rajl* is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) for *al-rajil* (the one on foot). Its counterpart is *al-rakb* and *al-sahb*.

As for ﴿wa-rajilika﴾, Hafs reads it as *rajilika*, with *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*, as in *ta'ib* and *ta'ib*, and its meaning is: and your gathering of those on foot. This is because the furthest that can be achieved in pursuing affairs is with horses and foot soldiers. It has been said that it is permissible for Iblis to have horses and men.

﴿And share with them in wealth and children﴾: al-Zajjaj said, every act of disobedience concerning wealth and children, Iblis is their partner in it, such as usury, forbidden gains, the *bahira* and the *sa'iba*, spending in sinfulness and extravagance, withholding zakat, seeking children through unlawful means, and naming children ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā and ʿAbd Shams.

﴿And promise them﴾: false promises, such as the intercession of the gods, honour before God through noble lineages, preferring the immediate over the deferred, and the like.

﴿But Satan promises them nothing except delusion﴾: it is the adorning of error with what makes it appear to be right.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 65:

﴿Indeed, My servants﴾ (the righteous ones), ﴿you have no authority over them﴾, meaning no power (yad) to change their faith, but only (you have the power) to beautify disobedience (taswil al-'isyan) for them. ﴿And your Lord is sufficient as a Guardian﴾, meaning: they entrust themselves to Him in seeking refuge from you, or He is a protector for them against you. All of this is a command of threat, so that he will be punished by it, or a command of humiliation; that is, that does not diminish My dominion.

Your Lord is He who drives for you the ships through the sea, that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed, He is ever Merciful to you.

Note: The quoted verse is 17:66, and the passage is the commentary on it.

Here is the translation of the commentary text:

﴿Your Lord is He who drives (yuzji)﴾, i.e., makes to run and sends along (yajri wa yusayyir), ﴿for you the ships in the sea that you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning: profit in trade. ﴿Indeed, He has always been Merciful to you﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 67:

﴿And when harm touches you at sea﴾, i.e., the fear of drowning, ﴿those whom you call upon vanish from you except Him﴾. Every one whom you call upon in your calamities vanishes from your minds, except Him alone, for you do not remember anyone other than Him. Or it means: those you call upon among the gods are lost, and fail to bring you relief; ﴿but Allah alone, whom you hope in﴾, is the exception here being disjunctive (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category as what precedes it). ﴿Then when He has brought you safely to land, you turn away﴾ from sincerity after deliverance, ﴿and man is ever ungrateful﴾, i.e., the disbeliever is ever ungrateful for favours.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 68:

﴿Do you then feel secure﴾ The hamzah (interrogative alif) is for denial (inkar), and the fa' is for conjunction (ʿatf) with an omitted element, whose estimated sense is: "Were you delivered, so that you felt secure?" Thus that led you to turn away. ﴿That He will not cause to sink with you a side of the land﴾ The word "jānib" (side) is in the accusative as an object of "yakhsifa" (cause to sink), like "the earth" in His words ﴿So We caused him and his house to sink into the earth﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. "Bikum" (with you) is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). The meaning: that He will cause a side of the land to sink, i.e., overturn it while you are upon it. The gist is that all sides are equal in His power, and for Him, in every side, whether land or sea, there is a means of destruction. The side of the sea is not exclusively His; rather, if drowning occurs on the side of the sea, then on the side of the land there is sinking (khasf), which is concealment beneath the earth, while drowning is concealment beneath the water. So it is incumbent upon the intelligent person that his fear of God be equal in all sides. And since ﴿or He will send against you a violent wind﴾ (ḥāṣib) is the wind that pelts (taḥṣibu), i.e., throws pebbles (ḥaṣbā'), meaning: or if He does not strike you with destruction from beneath you through sinking, He will strike you with it from above you, with a wind He sends against you, in which are pebbles. ﴿Then you will find for yourselves no guardian﴾ who would turn that away from you. (p-269)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 69:

﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not send you back into it another time, and then send against you⁠ ﴾ That is: Or do you feel secure that He will not strengthen your motives and supply your needs so that you return and board the sea from which He rescued you, and then you turn away, so that He takes vengeance upon you by sending against you ﴿a violent wind from the sea⁠﴾, which is the wind that has a crash (qasif), meaning an intense sound; or it is that which breaks the ship. ﴿So that He drowns you because of your disbelief⁠﴾, that is, because of your ingratitude for the blessing, which is your turning away when He rescued you. ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger in this matter⁠﴾, a tabi' meaning one who pursues a claim, from His saying ﴿so pursuit should be made in a fitting manner⁠﴾ (Qur'an 2:178), that is, a demand for retribution. The meaning is: We do what We do to them, and then they will not find anyone to demand from Us an account of what We have done, as a retaliation from Us and a取 of vengeance on Our part. This is similar to His saying ﴿and He does not fear its consequence⁠﴾ (Qur'an 91:15).

"an nakhsifa" (that He cause you to be swallowed up), "aw nursila" (or send), "an nu'idakum" (that He return you), "fa-nursila" (so He sends), "fa-nughriqakum" (so He drowns you) with the nun: Makki and Abu 'Amr.

And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam ﴿وَلَقَدْ كَرَّمْنا بَنِي آدَمَ﴾ with reason, speech, writing, a good form, an upright stature, the management of their livelihood and their return (to God), dominion, the subjugation of things, and eating food with their hands.

It is related from al-Rashid that food was brought to him and he asked for spoons. Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on him, was with him, and he said to him: "It has come in the tafsir of your grandfather Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿وَلَقَدْ كَرَّمْنا بَنِي آدَمَ﴾: 'We made for them fingers with which they eat.'" The spoons were brought, but he pushed them away and ate with his fingers.

﴿وَحَمَلْناهم فِي البَرِّ﴾: upon beasts; ﴿والبَحْرِ﴾: upon ships; ﴿وَرَزَقْناهم مِنَ الطَيِّباتِ﴾: with delicious things, or with what their hands have earned; ﴿وَفَضَّلْناهم عَلى كَثِيرٍ مِمَّنْ خَلَقْنا تَفْضِيلا﴾: that is, over all (of creation). This is like His saying ﴿وَأكْثَرُهم كاذِبُونَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:223], and al-Hasan said: "that is, all of them." Likewise His saying ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أكْثَرُهم إلا ظَنًّا﴾ [Yunus 10:36]. It is mentioned in al-Kashshaf that the intended sense of "most" (al-akthar) is "all."

And from him (ﷺ): "The believer is more honoured by God than the angels." This is because they (the angels) are created disposed to obedience, so in them there is intellect without desire, while in beasts there is desire without intellect, and in the child of Adam both are present. Whoever's intellect overcomes his desire is more honourable than the angels, and whoever's desire overcomes his intellect is worse than beasts. Moreover, He created everything for them, and created them for Himself.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 71:

﴿The day We call every people with their imam﴾: "The day" (yawma) is in the accusative, governed by "remember" (udhkur). ﴿Every people with their imam﴾: the bā' (with) is for the circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the implied sense is: "mixed together with their imam", that is, with those whom they followed, whether a prophet, a leader in religion, a book, or a religion. It will be said, "O followers of So-and-so! O people of such-and-such a religion, or of such-and-such a book!" It has also been said that it means "with the book of their deeds," so it will be said, "O companions of the book of good! O companions of the book of evil!" ﴿Then whoever is given his book in his right hand﴾ from among those who are called, ﴿those will read their book﴾. The word "those" (ulā'ika) was used because "whoever" (man) carries the sense of the plural. ﴿And they will not be wronged a thread﴾: they will not have the least thing reduced from their reward. He did not mention the disbelievers and the giving of their books in their left hands, being content with His saying [that is referred to above].

﴿Whoever is blind in this [world]﴾, the world, ﴿will be blind in the Hereafter﴾, likewise, ﴿and further astray in the way﴾ than the blind man. That is, more astray in path. The blind (al-a‘mā) is used metaphorically for one who cannot perceive visible things because his faculty is corrupted, applied to one who is not guided to the path of salvation. In this world, [he is blind] due to the loss of sight; in the Hereafter, because guidance to it will not benefit him. They have also permitted that the second [أَضَلُّ] be in the sense of the comparative (al-tafḍīl), as evidenced by its conjunction with [the word] "wa-aḍall" [and further astray]. For this reason Abū ‘Amr recited the first [أَعْمَى] with imālah (vocalizing the alif toward i, a practice called al-imālah, meaning a shift of the alif toward the vowel i) and the second [أَعْمَى in the comparative sense, i.e., أَضَلُّ] with tafkhīm (full, emphatic pronunciation), because the comparative form af‘al al-tafḍīl (the elative pattern used for comparison) is completed by "min" [than], so its alif is treated as though it occurs in the middle of the word, and therefore does not accept imālah. As for the first, nothing is attached to it, so its alif occurs at the end of the word, and thus it accepts imālah. Ḥamzah and ‘Alī [al-Kisā’ī] read both with imālah, and the rest [of the readers] read both with tafkhīm.

And when the Quraysh said, "Make the sign of mercy a sign of punishment, and the sign of punishment a sign of mercy, so that we may believe in you," there was revealed: ﴿And indeed they were close to tempting you﴾. (The "in" here is the light particle, a lightened form of the heavy inna, and the lam is the lam that distinguishes it from the negating particle.) The meaning: indeed the matter was such that they came close to tempting you, i.e., to deceive you, making you one who tempts them away ﴿from that which We have revealed to you﴾, of Our commands, Our prohibitions, Our promise and Our threat, ﴿so that you would fabricate against Us other than it﴾, that you would invent against Us what We have not said, meaning: what they had proposed, namely, turning the promise into a threat and the threat into a promise. ﴿And then they would have taken you as a close friend﴾, i.e., had you followed their desire, they would have taken you as a close friend, and you would have been their ally and would have left My protection.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 74:**

﴿And had We not made you firm⦆ — "And had it not been for Our making you firm," that is, Our steadfastness and Our protection (ʿismah) for you. ﴿You would almost have inclined toward them⦆ — you would have come close to leaning toward their deception (makr). ﴿A little⦆ — a slight inclination. This is an incitement from Allah to him (ﷺ), and an excellence of firmness (tathbit) bestowed upon him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 75:

﴿Otherwise﴾ if you had almost inclined toward them even a little, ﴿We would have made you taste a double portion of life and a double portion of death﴾. That is, We would have made you taste a doubled punishment in the Hereafter and a doubled punishment in the grave, because of the magnitude of your sin, given the nobility of your rank and your prophethood, as He said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30], and so on. The underlying sense of the statement is: "We would have made you taste the punishment of life and the punishment of death," because punishment is of two kinds: punishment at death, which is the punishment of the grave, and punishment in the life of the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the Fire. Punishment may be described as "doubled," as in His saying: ﴿So give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], meaning doubled. So the underlying sense is: "We would have made you taste a doubled punishment in life and a doubled punishment at death." Then the described noun was omitted, the attribute was put in its place, namely "doubling" (al-dif), and then the attribute was made into an idafah (construct phrase) as if it were the noun, so it was said "double of life" and "double of death." It is also permissible that by "double of life" is meant the punishment of the worldly life, and by "double of death" is meant what follows death of the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire. In the mention of the inclination and its minimization, together with the following of it with a severe threat of doubled punishment in both abodes, there is evidence that a wrong act's ugliness is magnified in proportion to the greatness of the status of the one who commits it. When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye."

﴿Then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾: one who assists you and would prevent Our punishment from you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 76:

﴿And indeed they were about to﴾ — that is, the people of Makkah — ﴿scare you﴾ — they would unsettle you with their enmity and their scheming — ﴿out of the land﴾ — out of the land of Makkah — ﴿so that they might expel you from it. And then they would not remain﴾ — they would not stay — ﴿after you﴾ — after you; that is, after your expulsion — ﴿except for a little [while]﴾ — a short time. Then God will destroy them. And so it was: they were destroyed at Badr, a little after his expulsion. Alternatively, its meaning is: "Had they expelled you, they would have been utterly uprooted, to the last man," but they did not expel him; rather, he emigrated by the command of his Lord. It was also said: "from the land of the Arabs," or "from the land of Madinah."

"Sunnata man qad arsalna qablaka min rusulina" (the way of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers). Meaning: whenever a people expelled their messenger from among them, it is God's way (sunnat Allah) to destroy them. It is put in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (nasb al-masdar al-mu'akkid), i.e., God established that as a way (sunnatan).

"Wa la tajidu li-sunnatina tahwilan" (and you will not find any change in Our way): tabdilan (substitution).

﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ means at its zawal (the sun's passing of its zenith). According to this view, the verse encompasses the five prayers. Or it means at its setting. According to this view, the noon (zuhr) and afternoon ('asr) prayers are excluded.

﴿until the darkness of the night﴾ is the darkness, and it is the time of the night (ʿishaʾ) prayer.

﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ refers to the dawn (fajr) prayer. It was called qurʾan, which means recitation, because recitation is a pillar (rukn) of it, just as it was called ruku' (bowing) and sujud (prostration). This is a proof against al-Asamm, who claimed that recitation is not a pillar. Or it was called qurʾān because of the length of its recitation. The phrase is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the prayer.

﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is witnessed﴾: it is witnessed by the angels of the night and of the day. These descend and those ascend. So it lies at the end of the record of the night and the beginning of the record of the day. Or it is witnessed by many of those who pray, as is customary.

(p-273)

And from the night, [also] some of it, ﴿perform tahajjud﴾ with it (the Qur'an) as a supererogatory prayer for you. Tahajjud (voluntary night vigil, literally abandoning sleep for prayer) is the abandoning of sleep for prayer, and it is also said that tahajjud can refer to sleep itself. ﴿With it﴾: with the Qur'an. ﴿Nafilah lak﴾: an additional act of worship for you beyond the five obligatory prayers. Nafilah is placed in the position of tahajjud, because tahajjud is an additional act of worship, so tahajjud and nafilah share one meaning. The meaning is: tahajjud was added for you beyond the obligatory prayers as a bounty for you, or as an obligation upon you specifically, to the exclusion of others, since for them it is a voluntary act. ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: it may be that He will raise you on the Day of Resurrection and establish you in a praiseworthy station. Or "yab'athaka" is taken to imply the meaning of "yuqimuka" (establish you). This station is, according to the majority, the station of intercession, and the reports indicate this. Or it is a station in which the banner of praise is given.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 80:**

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance, and cause me to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself an authority, a helper."﴾ "Sidq" (sound, truthful) here is a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: cause me to enter the grave with an entering that is pleasing, in a state of purity from slips; ﴿and cause me to exit a sound exit﴾, meaning: cause me to exit from it at the Resurrection (al-baʿth) with an exit that is pleasing, met with honour and safe from reproach. Its evidence is that He mentions it immediately after that resurrection. It has also been said that it was revealed when he was commanded to emigrate (hijra), intending the entry into Madina and the exit from Makkah. Or it is general, covering everything he enters into and is involved in, whether a matter or a place. ﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority, a helper﴾: a proof (ḥujja) that supports me against those who oppose me; or a kingdom and a strong power, helping Islam against unbelief and making it prevail over it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 81:**

﴿And say: The truth has come﴾, meaning Islam, ﴿and falsehood has vanished﴾, meaning it departed and perished, ﴿falsehood﴾, meaning polytheism; or, "the Qur'an has come and Satan has perished." ﴿Indeed, falsehood was ever bound to vanish﴾, meaning it was always bound to be annihilated at all times.

﴿And We send down﴾. With the lightened form (takhfif), Abu 'Amr reads it. ﴿of the Qur'an﴾: "min" here is for clarification (tabyin). ﴿that which is a healing﴾ from the diseases of the hearts, ﴿and a mercy﴾, a relief from distresses, a purification from faults, and an expiation of sins, ﴿for the believers﴾. And in a hadith: "Whoever does not seek healing through the Qur'an, may Allah not heal him" (p-274). ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers﴾, the disbelievers, ﴿except in loss﴾, that is, in misguidance, because of their denial of it and their disbelief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 83:

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾ with health and abundance, ﴿he turns away﴾ from the remembrance of Allah, or, when We bestow favour through the Qur'an, he turns away. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾ is an emphasis on the turning away, because turning away from a thing means to turn one's face's side away from it, whereas turning aside with the side means to bend one's flank away from it and turn one's back to it. Or it means arrogance, because that is the habit of the arrogant. "Nā'a" (nā, turned aside) is read with imāla (inclination) by Ḥamzah and with kasra by ʿAlī. ﴿And when evil touches him﴾ — poverty and sickness, or one of the calamities — ﴿he is despairing﴾, intensely hopeless of the mercy of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 84:

﴿Say: Each acts according to his own manner﴾ i.e., each person acts according to his own way (madhhab) and method (tariqah) that suits his state in guidance and misguidance. ﴿So your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way﴾ i.e., who is more upright in his path (madhhab) and method (tariqah).

﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is of the command of my Lord.﴾ That is: it is of a matter known to my Lord. The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that it is the soul that is in living beings. They asked about its reality, and He informed them that it is of the command of Allah, meaning of what He has kept exclusive knowledge of. It is related from Abu Hurayra: "The Prophet ﷺ passed away without knowing the soul." The earliest scholars were unable to grasp its quiddity even after spending long lifetimes engaged in discussing it. The wisdom in this is to show the intellect's inability to comprehend the knowledge of a created thing that is close to it, so that it becomes evident that it is even less able to comprehend its Creator. Accordingly, what has been said in defining it was rejected: that it is a subtle, airy body present in every part of the living being. It has also been said that it is a great spiritual creation, greater than the angel. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is Jibril, peace be upon him: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193] ﴿upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 194]. It is related from al-Hasan that it is the Qur'an, and the evidence for this is ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and because by it the hearts live. "Of the command of my Lord" means: of His revelation and speech, which is not the speech of humans. It is narrated that the Jews sent to the Quraysh, telling them to ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the soul: "If he answers all of them or remains silent about all of them, then he is not a prophet; but if he answers some and remains silent about others, then he is a prophet." So he explained to them the two stories and left the matter of the soul unspecified, though it is unspecified in the Torah too, and so they regretted their question. It has also been said that the question was about the creation of the soul, meaning: is it created or not? And His saying ﴿of the command of my Lord﴾ is evidence that the soul is created, so this was the answer. ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾. The address is general. It is related that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said this to them, they said: "Are we singled out by this address, or are you with us in it?" He said: "Rather, we and you alike have not been given of knowledge except a little." It has also been said that it is an address to the Jews specifically, because they said to the Prophet ﷺ: "We have been given the Torah, and in it is wisdom, and you have recited ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqara: 269]." So it was said to them that the knowledge of the Torah is little in comparison with the knowledge of Allah. Thus, little and much are relative matters. The wisdom that a servant is given is much good in itself, but when it is compared with the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, it is little.

Then He drew attention to the blessing of revelation and consoled him for patience in the face of the harm of disputation over the question, by His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾. "Surely take away" (lanadhhabanna) is the answer to an omitted oath, together with its substituting for the answer of the conditional clause; and the lam that enters upon "in" (in) is a preparatory lam (tawti'a) for the oath. The meaning: if We willed, We would take the Qur'an away and erase it from the breasts and the codices, leaving no trace of it. ﴿Then you would not find for yourself any guardian against Us in respect of it﴾. That is: then you would not find, after its being taken away, anyone who would take up a trust against Us to restore it to you, preserved and inscribed. (p-276)

That is: except that your Lord shows you mercy and returns it to you, as though His mercy relied upon it for its return. Or it is an exception of the disconnected type (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: but a mercy from your Lord has left it (the Qur'an) not taken away. This is a favour from God, the Exalted, in the Qur'an's remaining preserved after the great blessing of its revelation and its preservation in memory (*tahfiz*). It was revealed in reply to the words of al-Nadr: ﴿If we willed, we would say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31].

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 88:**

﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would never produce its like, even if they were helpers to one another."﴾ *(muʿīnan)*, meaning helper. The phrase ﴿they would never produce﴾, *lā yaʾtūna*, is the answer (*jawāb*) of a concealed oath (*qasam maḥdhūf*). Were it not for the preparatory *lam* (*al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾah*), it would be permissible for it to be the answer of the conditional clause, as in the verse of the poet:

*...... "He says: 'Neither is my property absent, nor am I one who is deprived.'"*

This is because the conditional clause is in the past tense. That is, "even if they backed one another to produce the like of this Qur'an in its eloquence, its beautiful composition and its arrangement, they would be unable to produce its like."

﴿وَلَقَدْ صَرَّفْنا﴾ [al-Isra': 41] "We have repeated and varied" (radadna wa-karrarna) ﴿لِلنّاسِ في هَذا القُرْآنِ مِن كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ "for the people in this Qur'an, from every example," meaning from every meaning that is like a parable in its strangeness and its beauty. ﴿فَأبى أكْثَرُ الناسِ إلا كُفُورًا﴾ "But most of the people refused except disbelief," meaning denial (juhudan). The construction ﴿فَأبى أكْثَرُ الناسِ إلا كُفُورًا﴾ is permitted, whereas "ḍarabtu illā Zaydan" (I struck no one but Zayd) is not, because أبى (abā, "refused") is interpreted (muta'awwil) as a negation, as if it had been said: "They were not pleased except with disbelief." When the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an became clear, and the other miracles were joined to it, and the proof was binding upon them and they were overcome, they proposed signs, in the manner of one who is stunned, confounded by the argument, and perplexed.

وقالوا: ﴿لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّى تَفْجُرَ لَنَا﴾. وبالتخفيف (أي قراءة الحرف المشدد بحرف واحد) قرأ الكوفي: ﴿مِنَ الْأَرْضِ﴾، أي: مكة، ﴿يَنْبُوعًا﴾: عينًا غزيرةً من شأنها أن تنبع بالماء لا تنقطع. وهي على وزن ﴿يَفْعُولٌ﴾، من: ﴿نَبَعَ الْمَاءُ﴾. (p-277)

﴿Or you have a garden of palm trees and grapes, and you cause the rivers to gush forth within it abundantly.﴾ The doubling (tashdid, gemination of the letter) here is agreed upon. ﴿The rivers within its midst﴾, meaning in its middle, ﴿a copious gushing﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 92:

﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed.﴾ With the *sin* vowelled with a fatha, it is read by al-Madani and ʿAsim, meaning *qiṭaʿan* (pieces). One says, "Give me a *kisfa* (piece) of this garment." With the *sin* sukun, it is read by the others, as the plural of *kisfa*, like *sidra* and *sidar* (lote-tree and lote-trees). They mean His saying: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or cause pieces (*kisaf*) of the sky to fall upon them.﴾ [Saba': 9]

﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a *qabil* (guarantor, surety)﴾: a *qabil* is one who vouches for what you say, a witness to its truth. The meaning is: or you bring God as a *qabil* and the angels as a *qabil*, like his saying:

"I was free of him, and my father..."

Or it means *muqabilan* (confronting, face to face), like *ʿashir* in the sense of *muʿashir* (companion), and similar. ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or do we see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21] Or it means a group (*jamaʿa*), as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the angels.

﴿Or you have a house of gold﴾ (dhahab, gold), ﴿or you ascend into the sky﴾ (tas'ad ilayha, you climb up to it), ﴿and we will not believe in your ascent﴾ (li-ajl ruqiyyika, on account of your ascent) ﴿until you bring down to us﴾ (wa bil-takhfif, Abu 'Amr reads it with takhfif, the lightened form, of tunazzilu) ﴿a book﴾ (ay: from the sky, in which is your confirmation) ﴿that we may read﴾ (naqra'uhu, an attribute of kitab). ﴿Say﴾ (qala, Makki and Shami read it as qala, meaning the Messenger said): ﴿Glory be to my Lord!﴾ (ta'ajjub, an expression of astonishment at their proposals to him). ﴿Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ (ay: I am a messenger like the other messengers, a human like them. The messengers used not to come to their peoples except with the signs that Allah made manifest through them, so the matter of the signs is not up to me; it is up to Allah. Why then do you choose them over me?) (p-278)

"And what prevented the people" — meaning the people of Makkah. The position of "an yu'minu" (that they believe) is accusative, as it is the second object of "mana'a" (prevented). "When the guidance came to them" — the Prophet and the Qur'an. "Except that they said" — the subject of "mana'a," and the sense is: what prevented them from believing in the Qur'an and in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) was nothing but their saying, "Has Allah sent a mortal as a messenger?" That is, nothing but a doubt that took root in their hearts, which is their denial that Allah would send a human being. The interrogative hamza in "a-ba'atha Allahu" is for denial, and what they denied is, in the matter of His wisdom, something objectionable.

Then Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Say: Had there been in the earth angels walking about securely⁠—﴾ walking on their feet as mankind walks, and not flying with their wings up to the heaven, so that they might hear from its inhabitants and know what is incumbent upon them. ﴿Content⁠﴾ is a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: dwelling in the earth, settled there. ﴿We would have sent down upon them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾ who would teach them good and guide them to the paths of right conduct. As for mankind, an angel is only sent to someone chosen from among them for prophethood, and that chosen one then carries out their summoning and guidance. And "a human" (basharan) and "an angel" (malakan) are circumstantial states (ḥālān) relating to "a messenger" (rasūlan).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 96:

﴿Say, "Allah suffices as a witness between me and you"﴾ that I have conveyed what I was sent with to you, and that you have denied and obstinately opposed it. "Shahidan" (as a witness) is a tamyiz (specification) or a hal (circumstantial accusative). ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants﴾ — the warners and those who are warned — ﴿Acquainted﴾, knowing their circumstances, ﴿Seeing﴾, observing their actions, so He will recompense them. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelievers.

"And whoever Allah guides, he is the one rightly guided." With the ya' (reading yahdi, "whom Allah guides"): Ya'qub, Sahl, and Abu 'Amr in agreement with them; and Madani in pause [wasl]. That is: whoever Allah enables to accept the guidance that exists, he is the one who is guided (al-muhtadi) in the sight of Allah. ﴿And whoever He leaves astray﴾, i.e., whoever He forsakes and does not protect, until he accepts the whisperings of Satan, ﴿you will not find for them protectors besides Him﴾, i.e., helpers. ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾, i.e., they will be dragged upon them, like His saying ﴿the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces﴾ [al-Qamar: 48]. "It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): How do they walk upon their faces? He said: Indeed, the One who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces." ﴿Blind, dumb, and deaf﴾, as they were in the world: they did not seek insight, did not speak the truth, and turned deaf ears to hearing it; so they are likewise in the Hereafter: they do not see what would gladden their eyes, do not hear what would delight their ears, and do not speak in a way that would be accepted from them. ﴿Their refuge is Hell; whenever it subsides﴾, i.e., its flame dies down, ﴿We increase them in blaze﴾, i.e., intensity of burning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 98:

﴿That is their recompense, because they disbelieved in Our signs and said: "When we have become bones and crumbled dust, shall we really be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ That is: that punishment is because they denied the restoration after annihilation. So Allah made their recompense that He set the Fire upon their parts, consuming them, and then restores them. They remain in that state, so that their regret over their denial of the Resurrection may increase.

Or have they not known? ﴿That God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them﴾ from among mankind, ﴿and has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt﴾, which is death or the Resurrection. ﴿Yet the wrongdoers refuse except with disbelief﴾, that is, denial despite the clarity of the proof.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 100:

﴿Say: "Even if you possessed﴾. Its underlying structure is: "Even if you yourselves possessed," because "law" (law, "if") enters upon verbs rather than nouns, so a verb must follow it. Thus the verb "tamlik" (possess) is elided, by way of explanatory omission, and the attached pronoun, which is the waw (the "-tum" of the verb), is replaced by the detached pronoun "antum" (you yourselves), because the attached element has dropped out of the wording. So "antum" is the subject of the elided verb, and "tamlikūna" (you possess) is its explanation. This is the aspect required by the science of grammar (i'rab). As for what the science of rhetoric (bayan) requires, it is that "antum tamlikūna" (you yourselves possess) contains an indication of exclusivity, and that people are the ones specifically characterized by extreme stinginess. ﴿the treasuries of my Lord's mercy﴾: His provision and all His blessings upon His creation. ﴿Then you would surely withhold, for fear of spending﴾.

That is: you would have been stingy, for fear that spending would exhaust it. ﴿And man has always been tight-fisted﴾: stingy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 101:

﴿And indeed We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾ On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him both: they are the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the stone, the sea, and the mountain that He lifted over the Children of Israel. And on the authority of al-Hasan: the flood, the years of drought, and the loss of fruits in place of the stone, the sea, and the mountain. ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾; that is, it was said to him: ask the Children of Israel (i.e., ask them about Pharaoh), and say to him: release the Children of Israel with me. His saying ﴿when he came to them﴾ is connected to the omitted statement; that is, "We said to him: ask them when he came to them." ﴿Pharaoh said to him: "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched"﴾; that is, you have been bewitched, so your mind has been confused.

Musa said: "You know well, O Pharaoh, that none has sent down these signs except the Lord of the heavens and the earth, their Creator, as clear proofs (basa'ir)." Here basa'ir is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning clear, manifest proofs, because you are obstinate, and similar. ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, in wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

The reading "ʿalimtu" with a ḍamma (ʿalimtu, "I know"), meaning: ʿAlī, that is: I am not bewitched as you described me; rather I am knowing of the soundness of the matter, and that these signs were sent down by the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Then he countered his assumption with his own assumption, saying: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are truly doomed (mathbur).﴾ It is as if he said: if you assume that I am bewitched, then I assume that you are doomed, and my assumption is more correct than yours, because it has a clear sign, which is your denial of what its soundness is known for and your obstinate rejection of the signs of God after their clarity. (p-281) As for your assumption, it is a pure lie, because your saying, while you know the soundness of my matter, that I do not think you are bewitched, is a false statement. Al-Farra' said: "mathbur" means turned away from good, from their saying: "What turned you away from this?" meaning: what prevented you and diverted you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 103:

﴿So Pharaoh intended﴾ ﴿to drive them﴾ out, i.e., Musa and his people, ﴿from the land﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt, or to banish them from the face of the earth through killing and extermination. ﴿So We drowned him and those with him, all of them.﴾ Thus his scheme recoiled upon him, for God drove him out by drowning him along with his Coptic people.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 104:

﴿And We said after him﴾ — after Pharaoh — ﴿to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land"﴾ — the land from which Pharaoh intended to drive you out ﴿. Then, when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ — i.e., the Resurrection ﴿, We shall bring you together in a mixed throng﴾ — all together, mingled with one another, you and them. ﴿Then We shall judge among you and distinguish between your blessed and your wretched.﴾ And al-lafif (the throng) means groups gathered from various tribes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 105:

﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended.﴾ And We did not send down the Qur'an except with wisdom (al-hikmah), and it did not descend except intertwined with truth and wisdom, because it includes guidance to every good. Or: We did not send it down from the sky except with the truth, preserved by the watch of the angels, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except preserved by them from the mixing-in of the devils. The narrator said: Muhammad ibn al-Sammak fell ill, so we took his urine and went with it to a Christian physician. A man of handsome face, pleasant scent, and clean clothing met us and said to us, "Where to?" We said to him, "To so-and-so the physician, to show him the urine of Ibn al-Sammak." He said, "Glory be to God! Do you seek help against the friend of God through the enemy of God? Strike it on the ground, and return to Ibn al-Sammak and tell him: place your hand on the place of the pain and say, ﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended.﴾" Then he went away from us and we did not see him. So we returned to Ibn al-Sammak and informed him of that, and he placed his hand on the place of the pain and said what the man had said, and he was healed at once. And he said, "That was al-Khidr, peace be upon him."

﴿And We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings﴾ of Paradise ﴿and a warner﴾ from the Fire.

Translation:

﴿And a Qur'an﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by ﴿We have divided it﴾ (faraqnahu), i.e., We have made it distinct (faṣṣalnāhu), or We have distinguished in it the truth from falsehood. ﴿That you might recite it to the people at a deliberate pace﴾, at a leisurely and steady rate. ﴿And We have sent it down in stages﴾, according to the occurrence of events.

﴿Say: Believe in it or do not believe.﴾ That is, choose for yourselves either the everlasting bliss or the painful punishment. Then he gave the reason with His words: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾, that is, the Torah before the Qur'an, ﴿when it is recited to them﴾, the Qur'an, ﴿they fall down upon their chins in prostration.﴾ "Prostrating" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 108:

﴿And they say: "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed the promise of our Lord has certainly been fulfilled."﴾ This is in connection with His saying ﴿Believe in it, or do not believe﴾ [al-Isra: 107]. That is: turn away from them, for if they do not believe in it and do not affirm the Qur'an, then indeed better than them are those who were given knowledge (al-'ulama') and who read the Scriptures (al-kutub), who have believed in it and affirmed it. So when it is recited to them, they fall down prostrating and glorify Allah, exalting His command and the fulfilment of what He promised in the revealed Scriptures and gave good news of, concerning the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him. This is what is meant by the promise mentioned. "In" (إنْ) is in the sense of "innahu" (indeed it), and it emphasises the verb just as "inna" (إنَّ) emphasises the noun. Just as "inna" was emphasised with the lam in ﴿innahum lamuhdaroon﴾ (indeed they will certainly be brought forth), so "in" is emphasised with the lam in ﴿lamaf'ulan﴾ (certainly fulfilled).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 109:

﴿And they fall down upon their chins, weeping﴾ The meaning of al-kharur (falling down) for al-dhaqan (the chin) is falling upon the face. He specified the chin because the nearest of things of his face to the ground during prostration is the chin. It is said: kharra ʿala wajhihi wa ʿala dhaqanihi, and kharra li-wajhihi wa li-dhaqanihi. As for the meaning of ʿala, it is apparent. As for the meaning of al-lam (li-), it is as if he made his chin and his face for falling down and specified it for that, since al-lam indicates specialization (ikhtisas). He repeated yakhirrūna li-l-adhqan because the two states differ: their falling down while they are prostrating, and their falling down while they are weeping. ﴿And it increases them﴾ the Qur'an ﴿in humility (khushuʿan)﴾, meaning softness of heart and moistness of the eye. (p-283)

**Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful** (﴿قُلِ ادْعُوا اللهَ أوِ ادْعُوا الرَحْمَنَ﴾). When Abu Jahl heard the Prophet saying, "O Allah, O Most Merciful," he said: "He forbids us to worship two gods, yet he calls upon two gods." So this was revealed. It is also said that the People of the Book said: "You mention the Most Merciful very little, while Allah has mentioned this name often in the Torah." So this was revealed. The *du'a* (calling upon) here means naming, not calling out. The *aw* (or) is for giving choice, meaning: name Him by this name or by that name, or mention Him by either one of them.

**Whichever you call upon** (﴿أيًّا ما تَدْعُوا﴾): the *tanwin* (nunation) on *ayyan* is a *'iwad* (substitute) for the omitted genitive complement, and *ma* was added for emphasis. *Ayyan* is in the accusative by *tad'u* (the verb), which is in the jussive by *ayyin* (the conditional particle). The meaning is: whichever of these two names you mention and name Him by.

**To Him belong the most beautiful names** (﴿فَلَهُ الأسْماءُ الحُسْنى﴾): the pronoun in *falahu* refers to the Essence of Allah, the Exalted. The *fa'* (then) is because this is the answer (*jawab*) of the conditional (*shart*). The meaning is: whichever you call upon, it is beautiful, so the statement *falahu al-asma' al-husna* was placed in its position. Because all His names are beautiful, these two names are beautiful too, since they are among them. The meaning of their being the most beautiful names is that they independently carry the meanings of glorification, sanctification and exaltation.

**Do not speak your prayer aloud** (﴿وَلا تَجْهَرْ بِصَلاتِكَ﴾): meaning, do not recite your prayer aloud. The genitive complement (*mudaf*) is omitted, because it causes no ambiguity, since loud and quiet are alternatives applied only to the voice. Prayer consists of actions and remembrances. It is reported: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to raise his voice in his recitation. When the polytheists heard it, they uttered nonsense and reviled, so he was commanded to lower his voice." The meaning is: do not speak loudly so that you make the polytheists hear.

**And do not speak it in a whisper** (﴿وَلا تُخافِتْ بِها﴾): so that you do not make those behind you hear.

**And seek a path between those** (﴿وَابْتَغِ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾): between loud and whispered. **A way** (﴿سَبِيلا﴾): a middle course. Or its meaning is: do not speak all of your prayer loudly, nor speak all of it in a whisper, but seek a path between these, by reciting aloud in the night prayer and whispering in the day prayer. Or "your prayer" means "your supplication."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 111:

﴿And say: "All praise is for Allah, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who has no ally out of weakness."﴾ As the Jews, the Christians and the Banu Malih claim [regarding a son], and as the polytheists claim [regarding a partner in the dominion]. That is: He is not humbled so as to need a helper, or He does not take an ally out of any humiliation He suffers, so that He might ward it off through that alliance. (p-284) ﴿And magnify Him with all magnification﴾: exalt Him and describe Him as being far greater than having a son or a partner. The Prophet (ﷺ) named this verse the "Verse of Honour" (Ayat al-Izz), and whenever a boy from the Banu Abd al-Muttalib became articulate, he would teach him this verse.
